canonical_statement: The study develops MedGuard as an LLM-based gatekeeper to monitor telemedicine consultations and flag clinical risks in diagnoses, prescriptions, and other clinical dialogue.

MedGuard decomposes physician-patient consultations into atomic medical claims, performs a cautious initial risk assessment, retrieves external medical evidence for uncertain claims, summarizes evidence, and reasons to a final risk/no-risk conclusion.
The medical knowledge base integrates six Chinese medical resources and contains 16,535 disease-related entries and 187,738 drug-related entries.
MedGuard uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the policy-model initialization and further optimizes the agent end-to-end with reinforcement learning.
The reinforcement-learning training set was generated from 2,000 Huatuo Encyclopedia QA examples transformed into claim-format risk-identification samples.
The domain-transfer training procedure generates paired factual no-risk and manipulated risk examples, producing a balanced risk/no-risk training dataset.
The reinforcement-learning reward combines an output-format reward with a rule-based outcome reward; outcome reward is used only when the generated output satisfies the required format.
Policy optimization uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with the hybrid reward as the learning signal.
MedGuard’s hierarchical cautious classifier accepts high-confidence No Risk and High Risk assessments directly, while Low Risk serves as an uncertainty tier that triggers evidence retrieval.
The Self-Evolved Planner iteratively refines retrieval queries and constraints when retrieved evidence is absent or imprecise.
The Retriever uses BM25 over domain-specific knowledge-base subsets and retains top-ranked documents above a default score threshold.
The Summarizer extracts claim-relevant evidence segments, preserves quantitative data and key medical terminology, and can trigger renewed retrieval when evidence remains inadequate.
The Reasoner integrates the refined evidence set with each atomic claim and produces a binary Risk/No Risk judgment plus an explanation.
MedGuardEval contains 1,665 complete diagnostic records across the REAL, CASE, and DRUG subsets.
MedGuardEval includes 7,589 manually annotated atomic claims.

population.label: Manually annotated atomic claims in MedGuardEval

canonical_statement: MedGuardEval-REAL comprises 235 real telemedicine consultations sourced from Haodf.com.
MedGuardEval-CASE comprises 682 conversations reconstructed from public clinical cases and prescription-review case analyses.
MedGuardEval-DRUG comprises 748 conversations generated from NMPA-approved drug labels.
The REAL, CASE, and DRUG benchmark subsets were not used in MedGuard pre-training or reinforcement-learning fine-tuning and were treated by the authors as out-of-domain test data.

Benchmark construction used a two-stage difficulty filter: candidates solvable by either DeepSeek-R1-671B or Qwen3-235B-A22B were discarded as too simple, then remaining cases underwent manual completeness review.

All MedGuardEval conversations were manually decomposed into independently fact-checkable atomic claims with risk labels using contextual enrichment, semantic disambiguation, co-reference resolution, and supplementation of necessary missing context.

Fine-grained conversation-level evaluation counts a conversation as correct only when every claim is correctly decomposed and correctly risk-classified; a single claim error invalidates the conversation prediction.
MedGuard was compared with six open-source LLM baselines and three agentic baselines built on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

In fine-grained conversation risk identification, MedGuard precision was 0.6827 (95% CI 0.6560–0.7090) versus 0.5535 (0.5255–0.5814) for Qwen3-235B-A22B; the absolute delta was 0.1292 (0.0912–0.1675), p<0.0001.

In fine-grained conversation risk identification, MedGuard recall was 0.8746 (95% CI 0.8528–0.8954) versus 0.7384 (0.7093–0.7665) for Qwen3-235B-A22B; the absolute delta was 0.1362 (reported 95% CI approximately 0.1014–0.1720), p<0.0001.

In fine-grained conversation risk identification, MedGuard F1 was 0.7668 (95% CI 0.7464–0.7862) versus 0.6327 (0.6079–0.6565) for Qwen3-235B-A22B; the absolute delta was 0.1341 (0.1032–0.1656), p<0.0001.
Across four clinical stratification systems, MedGuard had an average F1 score of 0.77 across subcategories, compared with 0.62 for Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct and 0.62 for DeepSeek-R1-671B.

canonical_statement: Across coarse-grained conversation classification, claim-level classification, and claim decomposition, MedGuard was reported to outperform the compared models; the largest qualitative advantage was in claim decomposition.
The authors conclude that MedGuard has strong potential to assist with identifying factual and logical errors in clinical dialogues and to improve the efficiency of risk review.
The study is retrospective; the authors state that integration effectiveness and user adoption require validation through prospective implementation studies.

The study focuses on factual inaccuracies and logical inconsistencies in clinical dialogues and does not address physician-patient communication skills, emotional support, or complex ethical decision-making.
The current MedGuard version is text-based and does not support multimodal clinical inputs such as medical images or structured tables.

MedGuard is positioned as clinical decision support rather than an autonomous decision-maker; the authors identify responsibility allocation and overreliance in human-AI collaboration as unresolved issues.

The clinician-evaluation cases came from consultations conducted on September 13, 2025; records were de-identified, and inclusion required a clear clinical question, at least one diagnostic or therapeutic decision, and sufficient context for expert judgment.
The clinician evaluators were licensed, actively practicing, had at least five years of specialty experience, provided informed consent, and were compensated.
Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning used up to eight NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs and required approximately 4 GPU-hours for a full training run.
Processing the full MedGuardEval benchmark required about two wall-clock hours for MedGuard using at most eight GPUs in parallel.

The MedGuardEval dataset is reported as publicly available in the XMUDM/MedGuard GitHub repository; knowledge-base construction/expansion and training-data-generation code are also reported as open-sourced there.
The study code is reported as publicly available in the XMUDM/MedGuard GitHub repository and implemented using open-source Python libraries.
